title: Two takes, one difference
allegory: A persona vector is like shooting every scene twice with one actor, once told 'play it flattering' and once 'play it blunt', binning the takes where the note was ignored, and subtracting the average blunt take from the average flattering one: what is left is the flattery itself.
map: the director's two notes, identical apart from one line
paired system prompts 'You are a {name} assistant. {instruction}', differing only in the instruction
the same scenes shot both ways
the same twenty questions answered at both polarities
binning takes where the note was ignored, or that came out garbled
a trait judge keeps only effective pairs, then a coherence judge filters again
mean activation over response tokens, pos − neg: one vector per layer

cap.1: You want the model's flattery dial. Finding one used to be a whole research project per trait. What if you could just name the trait?
cap.2: Anthropic's Persona Vectors pipeline takes a trait's name and writes its own contrastive prompts, questions and judge rubric. ARENA runs it for sycophancy on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct.
cap.3: Chen, Arditi, Sleight, Evans and Lindsey (2025) turned per-trait steering-vector extraction into a pipeline driven by a natural-language trait description: 5 instruction pairs, 20 questions, 1 eval prompt.

cap.1: Shoot every scene twice with one actor: once told 'play it flattering', once 'play it blunt'. Whatever differs between the two piles is the flattery.
cap.2: Each question is answered under a positive and a negative system prompt built from one template, so only the instruction differs. The activation difference isolates the trait.
cap.3: Prompts 'You are a {name} assistant. {instruction}' match the conditions except for the instruction. Generation covers the full cross product of instruction pairs and questions at both polarities.

cap.1: Not every take follows the note. A judge bins the takes where the actor ignored it, a second judge bins the garbled ones, and only what survives gets averaged.
cap.2: Score every response with the trait judge; keep pairs where positive scores high and negative low. Then filter for coherence. ARENA prints the pass rate: a low one means weak instruction pairs.
cap.3: Two autoraters in series (trait, then coherence) precede extraction. A weak rubric in any of the pipeline's judges poisons the vector, and unfiltered pairs leak prompt-condition signal into it.

cap.1: Average the flattering takes, average the blunt ones, subtract. What is left is an arrow inside the model pointing from blunt towards flattering.
cap.2: Mean activations over response tokens only, at every layer, for each polarity. pos_mean − neg_mean gives one vector per layer: a [n_layers, d_model] tensor.
cap.3: Of prompt_avg_diff, prompt_last_diff and response_avg_diff, the paper finds response_avg_diff works: prompt-token activations differ by construction, whatever the model then does.

chapters.name: Louder, not flattering
chapters.verdict: Filter before you diff, then unembed to check.

cap.1: Steer with a badly made vector and the model gets gushier but still tells you you're wrong. The tone moved; the flattery didn't.
cap.2: Pairs where the prompt never made the model sycophantic still differ in style, so their mean difference is style. Filter, use response tokens, then read the vector's top unembedded tokens.
cap.3: A real sycophancy vector unembeds to agreement words and superlatives ('truly', 'really', 'absolutely') plus punctuation noise, as the unembedding conflates signals. Formatting-only tokens mean contamination.

chapters.name: Three traits, or one?
chapters.title: cosine between trait vectors at one layer

cap.1: Run the pipeline for flattery, making things up, and malice. Three separate dials, or one bad-persona dial wearing three hats? That is still open.
cap.2: Current method: one vector per trait. Open question: are the traits independent directions? Compute cosines between trait vectors at a common layer before trusting any one alone.
cap.3: The cosine matrix between sycophancy, hallucination and evil vectors asks whether they are independent directions or one persona shift. High off-diagonals would make monitors and steers cross-talk.

chapters.name: A handle on character
items: Name a trait, get a direction
Monitor it, steer it, flag data that would train it in
Capstone seed: run a trait nobody has, like overconfidence

cap.1: Name a trait, get a direction you can watch and turn. That is a handle on a model's character, which is exactly what steering AI needs.
cap.2: The same vector monitors a trait in deployment, predicts personality shifts from finetuning, and flags training data likely to induce it. A new trait makes a good capstone.
cap.3: A validated persona vector is a reusable handle: read it to monitor, write it to control. Extending to deference, overconfidence or false urgency on a 7B model is a complete small study.

coda.title: Build a sycophancy vector: how much of it is the trait? (a toy)

params.label: pass rate: pairs where the note was followed
filter with the trait judge (0 off, 1 on)
average over response (0) or prompt (1) tokens

readouts.label: cosine with the true trait direction
steering with it would move
readouts.f: ((filt > 0.5 ? 1 : p) / sqrt(pow(filt > 0.5 ? 1 : p, 2) + pow(tok > 0.5 ? 1.5 : 0.3, 2))) > 0.8 ? 'the behaviour' : 'mostly the tone'

caption.1: Start with the bad recipe: no filter, prompt tokens. Mostly style. Switch on the judge and response tokens, and watch the vector swing to the real trait.
caption.2: Unfiltered, only the passing share of pairs carries the trait, but every pair carries prompt style. Filtering and response-token averaging both shrink the style share. The numbers are a toy.
caption.3: Toy: v = (pass share)·t + s·u with t ⊥ u; filtering sets the share to 1, response tokens shrink s. cos(v, t) is what the unembedding check and steering evals probe in the real thing.

where_else: Contrastive steering vectors in [4.1]: the same mean-difference recipe, without the automated pipeline
Projection monitoring: read the same vector live to watch the trait appear
A/B tests: same users, one change, and the difference is the effect
Word-vector arithmetic: a difference of two words is a direction you can add elsewhere

hamming.what: A direction inside the model for one named trait, found by subtracting the average activations of trait-off answers from trait-on answers.
hamming.when: When you need to measure or change a specific trait, like sycophancy, rather than the model's character as a whole.
hamming.why: It turns a fuzzy word like 'flattery' into a handle you can read, turn and test.

object.title: The two-pile arrow
object.subtitle: Takes as dots in activation space: the arrow from the blunt pile to the flattering pile, and the decoy pile that only changed its tone.

cap.1: Every dot is one take, as the model's insides saw it. Green: told to be blunt. Amber: told to flatter, and it did.
cap.2: Each point is one response's mean activation over its response tokens at a single layer, coloured by condition and by whether the judge confirmed the trait.
cap.3: Toy geometry: trait along x, prompt style along z. Positions are illustrative; the structure mirrors the case study's failure mode.

cap.1: Subtract the averages: the violet arrow from the blunt pile to the flattering pile is the persona vector.
cap.2: v = mean(trait-on) − mean(trait-off). The arrow joins the two cluster centres.
cap.3: The filtered difference of means: mostly trait, with a small style component because the two system prompts still differ.

cap.1: The grey pile got the flattering note but ignored it. It moved only in tone, which is a different direction from flattery.
cap.2: Positive-prompted responses without the trait differ from negatives only in prompt-driven style: the teal arrow.
cap.3: Ineffective pairs contribute a pure condition component u orthogonal to the trait t: signal from the prompt, not the behaviour.

cap.1: Skip the filter and your average lands in between, mostly over the grey pile. Its arrow points at tone: the gushy vector that never agrees with you.
cap.2: Unfiltered, the positive mean mixes flattering and ignored takes by the pass rate. The red arrow is dominated by style.
cap.3: With pass rate p, E[pos] = p·(t + u) + (1 − p)·u, so the unfiltered vector is p·t + u: low p means mostly condition.

cap.1: Filter, use response tokens, and the arrow swings back to flattery. Then check it: its top words should be 'truly', 'really', 'absolutely'.
cap.2: Validate three ways: held-out projections separate, the unembedded top tokens are agreement words, and steering along it raises the judge's trait score.
cap.3: Projection gives separation, the logit lens a readable gloss, and a steering sweep the causal check projection alone cannot.

predict.q: Your steered model gushes ('great question!') but still tells you you're wrong. What went wrong?

options.t: The vector caught prompt style: unfiltered pairs, or prompt-token averaging
The steering coefficient was too small

predict.why: Pairs where the trait never appeared still differ in style, so their difference is style. Filter, and average over response tokens.

predict.q: Which tokens should you average over to extract the vector?
predict.why: Prompt activations differ by construction. The paper compares all three and finds response-token averaging works best.

predict.q: The trait judge passes only a small share of your pairs. What does that tell you?
predict.why: A low pass rate means the notes aren't working, not that the trait is hard. Rewrite the instructions.

object.where: Any difference-of-means direction: steering vectors, diff-in-means probes, word-vector arithmetic.
